observations.statement: The core defines seven UI-command-to-handler mappings: topic open, rename, reopen, reorder, split, annotation resolve, and annotation upsert. Every mapping declares an empty expected_event_types array.
Every command's effect prose requires an explicit no-persist receipt or route/open disposition and rejects placeholder command_applied events.

Each command names an availability selector and disabled-reason projection, while its accessibility block covers role/name/description, keyboard activation, focus handling, and disabled-state announcement.

Production certification names render/control, dispatcher, typed-contract, state-projection, disabled-reason, receipt/event, accessibility, and regression evidence categories; the concrete test requirements restate dispatcher, state, effect, and accessibility obligations.

candidate_findings.title: Typed payload and result contracts remain alternatives rather than exact contracts
candidate_findings.statement: For all seven commands, the core requires a typed payload/result contract or an explicit route/open no-persist disposition, but it neither selects the applicable branch nor states payload fields, validation rules, result variants, or result meanings. The same wiring can therefore be implemented with incompatible command interfaces while satisfying the literal alternative.
candidate_findings.impact: GUI callers, dispatcher fixtures, and handlers can disagree on arguments and results, preventing deterministic implementation and certification.

candidate_findings.title: Mutation-labeled commands have no authoritative state-change or postcondition contract
candidate_findings.statement: Topic rename, reopen, reorder, split, annotation resolve, and annotation upsert each declare no expected event type and describe only a no-persist receipt or route/open disposition. The core does not specify whether these commands perform a mutation, merely initiate another interaction, or delegate mutation elsewhere, nor does it identify an authoritative postcondition.
candidate_findings.impact: A builder could implement no mutation, transient local mutation, or an unmodeled external mutation and still produce the required receipt, leaving user-visible behavior and state authority indeterminate.

candidate_findings.title: Availability and disabled-reason paths lack state semantics
candidate_findings.statement: The core names selector paths but does not define their value types, availability states, transition rules, loading or stale behavior, precedence, or the conditions producing each disabled reason.
candidate_findings.impact: Controls can disagree about visibility, enablement, dispatch guards, and disabled copy while reading the same nominal paths.

candidate_findings.title: Accessibility obligations do not define executable expected values
candidate_findings.statement: The accessibility blocks require a stable role/name/description, keyboard activation, deterministic focus return, and disabled announcement, but do not identify the concrete role, accessible name or description, activation keys, focus destination, visibility rules, or announcement behavior.
candidate_findings.impact: Materially different controls and regression assertions can all claim compliance, including implementations with incompatible keyboard and focus behavior.

candidate_findings.title: Receipt and failure lifecycle behavior is unspecified
candidate_findings.statement: The core requires dispatch evidence and a no-persist receipt, and it mentions focus behavior after error, but it does not define receipt fields or authority, success versus failure receipts, cancellation, timeout, retry, duplicate-dispatch, idempotency, or error-result behavior.
candidate_findings.impact: Handlers, consumers, tests, and GUI recovery logic can make incompatible choices about whether a command completed and whether it is safe to retry.

candidate_findings.title: Certification evidence is categorical rather than an exact acceptance oracle
candidate_findings.statement: The evidence contract names evidence categories, while the test requirements assert only that routing, selector reads, receipt prose, and accessibility categories are demonstrated. They do not provide concrete inputs, expected result values, pre-state, post-state, negative cases, or failure expectations.
candidate_findings.impact: Different fixtures can certify different behaviors under identical test IDs, so the named evidence does not close the exact-behavior gaps.

explicit_non_gaps.statement: The UI command identifiers and handler targets are explicitly mapped for every command in the core.
Concrete selector paths for availability and disabled-reason projection are present for every command.
The core explicitly rejects placeholder command_applied events and requires no unexpected persisted domain event for the sampled boundary commands.
Dispatcher, state-projection, effect, and accessibility evidence categories and test identifiers are explicitly present.

unknowns.statement: The exact payload fields, field types, validation constraints, and success and failure result variants for each command are unknown within this window.
The intended state transition and observable success postcondition for rename, reopen, reorder, split, annotation resolve, and annotation upsert are unknown within this window.
The type, state domain, derivation authority, transition behavior, and disabled-reason vocabulary behind the named selector paths are unknown within this window.
Concrete accessible roles, names, descriptions, activation keys, focus destinations, and announcement mechanics are unknown within this window.
Receipt schema, producer authority, consumer, correlation validation, replay behavior, and terminal failure behavior are unknown within this window.
Beyond the named handler paths, the authority responsible for any durable state change and the consumers responsible for applying or displaying command results are unknown within this window.
